```{r setup, include = FALSE}
  collapse  = TRUE,

```

autoSpectra predicts soil properties (organic carbon, clay, pH, nitrogen and
30 others) from VisNIR or MIR spectra. It uses models trained on the
[Open Soil Spectral Library](https://soilspectroscopy.org) (OSSL v1.2).

This guide covers the usual path: getting your spectra into the right shape,
downloading the models, predicting, and reading the result, including
how far to trust it.

```{r load}
library(autoSpectra)
```

## The model families

Each spectral domain has a Cubist family, a PCA-VAE family, and PCA-VAE
families for single instrument windows. All are trained on the same OSSL data
and predict the same properties.

| Family | Sensor | Method | Prediction intervals |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist` | VisNIR, 400–2500 nm | Cubist + PCA(120) | yes |
| `OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE` | VisNIR, 400–2500 nm | soilVAE ensemble on PCA(120) | yes |
| `OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE_800`, `_1000`, `_1350` | VisNIR, from 800, 1000 or 1350 to 2500 nm | the same, one window | yes |
| `OSSL_MIR_Cubist`    | MIR, 600–4000 cm⁻¹  | Cubist + PCA(120) | yes |
| `OSSL_MIR_PCAVAE`    | MIR, 600–4000 cm⁻¹  | soilVAE ensemble on PCA(120) | yes |
| `OSSL_MIR_PCAVAE_700_3800` | MIR, 700–3800 cm⁻¹ | the same, one window | yes |

```{r registry}
names(model_registry)
get_family("OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist")$citation
```

- **Cubist + PCA** replicates the method of Safanelli et al. (2025) and needs
  no Python. It is the family validated on held-out datasets (see *How far to
  trust the predictions*).
- **PCA-VAE** takes exactly the same input as Cubist and replaces only the
  regression model with an ensemble of five supervised VAEs from the
  soilVAE package. On a full-range instrument it is the more accurate choice.
- **The window families** are the PCA-VAE trained on the range of a real
  instrument. `predict_soil_agnostic()` sends each spectrum to the widest
  window it covers, so instruments that cover only part of the range are
  predicted too, provided their optical response resembles the benchtop
  instruments in OSSL. No OSSL family transfers to a handheld unit with a
  different response, such as the NeoSpectra (tested on 13 units: the
  predictions fail, and every scan is flagged out of domain).

## Your spectra

`predict_soil()` takes a data frame with:

- a `Soil_ID` column, and
- one numeric column per band, **named by its wavelength (nm) or wavenumber
  (cm⁻¹)**: `"350"`, `"352"`, …

What the values should be:

- **VisNIR:** reflectance, as a fraction (0–1) or a percentage (0–100). The
  package converts it to absorbance itself.
- **MIR:** absorbance.

You do not need to match the model's band spacing or range. Spectra are
resampled to the model's grid automatically.

Here are two small synthetic data sets standing in for real measurements. One
is from a full-range laboratory instrument, the other from an instrument
covering 908–1676 nm.

```{r synthetic}
set.seed(1)
make_spectra <- function(wl, n, prefix) {
  M <- t(vapply(seq_len(n), function(i)
    0.25 + 0.1 * i / n + 0.05 * sin(wl / 180) -
      0.08 * exp(-((wl - 1900) / 60)^2) +
      rnorm(length(wl), sd = 0.002),
    numeric(length(wl))))
  df <- data.frame(Soil_ID = sprintf("%s_%02d", prefix, seq_len(n)), M,
                   check.names = FALSE)
  names(df)[-1] <- as.character(wl)
  df
}

lab      <- make_spectra(seq(350, 2500, by = 2), n = 5, prefix = "lab")
handheld <- make_spectra(seq(908, 1676, by = 6), n = 5, prefix = "micro")

lab[1:3, 1:5]
```

```{r plot-spectra}
plot_spectra(lab, family = get_family("OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist"),
             title = "Synthetic full-range VisNIR spectra")
```

### How partial coverage is handled

When your instrument covers only part of a model's range, the bands it does
not measure become missing after resampling. Rather than guess them,
`predict_soil_agnostic()` uses the window family whose whole grid your
spectra cover. Here is which windows each synthetic instrument covers:

```{r coverage}
windows <- c("OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE", "OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE_800",
             "OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE_1000", "OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE_1350")
covers <- function(df, fid) {
  wl <- get_wavelengths(df)
  X  <- resample_to_grid(as.matrix(df[, wl$cols]), wl$wl,
                         get_family(fid)$wavegrid)
  all(is.finite(X))
}
sapply(windows, function(f) c(lab = covers(lab, f),
                              micro = covers(handheld, f)))
```

The full-range spectra fit the widest window, 400–2500 nm, and are predicted
by the full-range PCA-VAE. The 908–1676 nm unit stops short of every window:
`predict_soil_agnostic()` leaves its rows as `NA` and warns. For such an
instrument, train a model on its own spectra with `train_sensor_model()`.

## Download the models

The trained models are published on
[Zenodo](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23950129). You download them once.
Each family is fetched on its own (tens of MB) from the GitHub release of the
latest Zenodo version and checked against its SHA256 sum; only if GitHub cannot
be reached does the package fall back to the full Zenodo archive (2.6 GB).
They are stored in `default_model_dir()`, a folder in
`tools::R_user_dir("autoSpectra", "data")`, or wherever
`options(autoSpectra.model_dir = ...)` points.

```{r download, eval = FALSE}
download_ossl_models("OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist")   # one family
download_ossl_models(c("OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE", "OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE_800",
                       "OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE_1000", "OSSL_VisNIR_PCAVAE_1350"))
download_ossl_models()                       # default families
download_ossl_models("all")                  # every published family

models_available()
```

The PCA-VAE and window families also need the soilVAE package and its
Python backend. The Cubist families need only the `Cubist` package.

```{r keras, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("soilVAE")
soilVAE::vae_install()
```

## Predict

```{r predict, eval = FALSE}
my_spectra <- readxl::read_excel("my_visnir_spectra.xlsx")

pred <- predict_soil(my_spectra, "OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist",
                     properties = c("oc", "clay.tot", "ph.h2o"),
                     with_pi    = TRUE)
format_predictions(pred)

# Any instrument range: one PCA-VAE window per spectrum
pred_any <- predict_soil_agnostic(my_spectra, "visnir",
                                  properties = c("oc", "clay.tot", "ph.h2o"))
table(pred_any$model_family)
```

The result has one row per sample and one column per property, in the
property's original units. Use `property_label()` to look up a unit:

```{r labels}
sapply(c("oc", "clay.tot", "ph.h2o"), property_label)
```

With `with_pi = TRUE`, the Cubist and PCA-VAE families add `<property>_lo` and
`<property>_hi` columns. They give a 68% prediction interval by default; set
it with `confidence =`. The intervals are conformal and scaled to each
sample, so samples the model finds harder get wider intervals.

### Check the applicability domain

A prediction is only as good as the model's familiarity with the spectrum.
`predict_applicability()` flags samples that fall outside the training
data:

```{r ad, eval = FALSE}
ad <- predict_applicability(my_spectra, "OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist", prop = "oc")
head(ad)              # score, threshold, in_domain
plot_applicability(ad)
```

Every OSSL family checks two distances on its 120 principal components. The
Q-statistic is the residual the components cannot reproduce: features the
training spectra do not have. Hotelling T2 is the distance along the
components: known features in unusual proportions. Each limit is the 99th
percentile of the training spectra, and a spectrum is in domain when it
passes both (`in_domain_q`, `in_domain_t2` and `t2` show each check). Treat
out-of-domain predictions with caution, whatever the interval says.

## How far to trust the predictions

The number that matters is how a model does on soils from a source it never
saw, not on a random sample of its own training data. We measure this
with **leave-one-dataset-out (LODO)** validation: each OSSL contributing
dataset is held out in turn.

Weighted R² under LODO, Cubist families:

| Property | VisNIR | MIR |
|---|---|---|
| Organic carbon (`oc`)    | 0.63 | 0.83 |
| Total nitrogen (`n.tot`) | 0.47 | 0.68 |
| pH in water (`ph.h2o`)   | 0.63 | 0.76 |
| Clay (`clay.tot`)        | 0.41 | 0.16 |

On a random held-out split of the same data, the same models score R²
0.82–0.99 for every one of these, in line with the 10-fold results Safanelli
et al. (2025) report. That gap is the difference between predicting soils like
the training data and predicting soils from a new source. Expect the LODO
figures when your samples come from a region or laboratory that is not in the
OSSL. Clay from MIR transfers particularly poorly.

The README has the full tables, including the side-by-side comparison with
Safanelli et al. (2025), whose 10-fold results the Cubist family reproduces.

### Why predictions cannot explode

Organic carbon, nitrogen and most other concentrations are modelled on a
`log1p` scale and transformed back with `expm1()`. That inverse is
exponential: a modest error on the log scale becomes an enormous one in
original units. For this reason, autoSpectra bounds every prediction to
the range the model was calibrated on before transforming back:

```{r bounded}
# A model calibrated on organic carbon between 0.1% and 30%
y_train <- apply_target_transform(c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 12, 30), "oc")
bounds  <- target_bounds(y_train)

# Three predictions on the log scale; the last is far outside calibration
y_hat <- log1p(c(3, 40, 4000))

expm1(y_hat)                                         # unbounded
invert_target_transform(y_hat, "oc", bounds = bounds) # what autoSpectra returns
```

A prediction outside the calibration range is capped near its edge
rather than extrapolated. This is not a fix for a bad prediction: the
applicability-domain check is what tells you a sample is unfamiliar.

## The OSSL data

autoSpectra never redistributes OSSL data. The published models contain only
model parameters and aggregate statistics. Every release archive is checked
by `audit_release_archive()` before it is uploaded.

To retrain the models yourself, the data are downloaded from the official OSSL
storage bucket into a cache in your user directory:

```{r retrain, eval = FALSE}
ossl_download()            # about 2 GB, cached locally
ossl_cache_dir()           # where it went

train_ossl_models("OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist", properties = "oc")
```

## Interactive use

For point-and-click prediction, the package includes a Shiny app:

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
run_autoSpectra()
```

## Citing

```{r cite, eval = FALSE}
citation("autoSpectra")
```

If you use the OSSL data or the pre-trained models, also cite the OSSL. If
you use the Cubist families, also cite Safanelli et al. (2025),
<doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0296545>.
